title: What’s new in AI infrastructure and orchestration in October
raw_text: The Google Cloud AI Infrastructure team had another busy month in October, filled with new product launches and updates to power today’s AI and agentic workloads scalably and efficiently. We were also honored to share our progress with customers, partners, and the broader community at leading industry events, including NVIDIA GTC, PyTorch Conference, and AGNTCon + MCPCon. Let’s dive in! Product, technology, and tools updates New compute service: Agent Compute Engine is a purpose-built compute service providing high-performance, hardware-isolated microVM sandboxes alongside expanded agent governance capabilities like Agent Gateway and Agent Registry, all in the service of securing and scaling autonomous AI agents. Its primary benefits include rapid sub-second activation, extreme workload density through copy-on-write memory sharing, enterprise-grade security and identity management, and cross-cloud observability. AI Hypercomputer updates: At NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 we announced updates to our agentic infrastructure, including to A5X instances powered by the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, Virgo Network scale-out fabric, and Managed Lustre storage. These co-engineered advancements provide enterprises with accelerated performance, enhanced sovereign AI controls, while advanced Confidential Computing capabilities help you train and deploy complex multi-step models securely and efficiently. GKE product update: CPU startup boost for GKE , in preview, uses Kubernetes In-place Pod Resize to dynamically elevate container CPU resources during initialization and scale them back down to steady-state levels without having to restart the containers. This feature removes startup throttling and accelerates cold starts by up to 2x for demanding workloads, helping to lower cloud infrastructure costs. GKE product update: The preview of the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) brings low-touch deployment, automated lifecycle management, enterprise credential security, and fleet-wide governance to Wiz's eBPF runtime threat detection for both Standard and Autopilot GKE clusters. Modernization tools: Together at last. Google Cloud Modernize brings Google Cloud’s migration and modernization tools, including Migration Center, Google Cloud VMware Engine, Google Cloud Mainframe Modernization and our new EKS-to-GKE Migration Agent, into a single portfolio. Enterprise teams now have purpose-built agentic capabilities across infrastructure assessment, platform modernization, and application modernization. Cloud Run product update: Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run automatically scale worker pools based on Temporal task queue demands and scale down to zero when idle. This integration eliminates cluster management, lowers costs, using Temporal Worker Versioning to safely handle stateful, long-running workflows and AI agent workloads. New open-source product: llm-d 1.0 is an open-source, Kubernetes-native serving stack that turns a cluster of model servers into a coordinated serving pool, unifying distributed LLM inference across mixed Google Cloud TPU and GPU fleets. Co-founded by Google and partners, it provides production-ready benefits such as cache-aware routing, tiered KV cache offloading, and priority-based flow control to dramatically improve context reuse, reduce time-to-first-token latency, and efficiently scale multi-tenant agent workloads. New open-source product: Working with Meta, we open-sourced TorchTPU , a native PyTorch stack that integrates Google TPUs directly into the PyTorch ecosystem alongside GPUs and CPUs. Now developers can train, serve, and deploy models natively on TPUs using familiar frameworks like Hugging Face, vLLM, and TorchTitan. Google Distributed Cloud updates: Organizations that operate under strict sovereignty mandates would love to use AI to help them process data, but can’t send it to the cloud. The latest version of Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) air-gapped brings frontier AI models and multimodal enterprise search with Gemini into these isolated environments. In addition, GDC air-gapped supports NVIDIA HGX B300 systems based on the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra architecture, and features enhanced networking and security capabilities. Edge inference product: Google open-sourced ML Drift , a cross-platform on-device GPU compute engine built for LiteRT that abstracts hardware complexities across OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal, and WebGPU. The framework delivers peak performance, enhanced 5D tensor support, and memory efficiency for both classical machine learning workloads and advanced generative AI models at the edge. Open-weight model support: Reflection's Beam is an open-weight, 501-parameter model released under an Apache 2.0 license designed specifically for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. We announced day 0 support and ready-to-run deployment recipes for service Beam on AI Hypercomputer and NVIDIA AI Infrastructure. Practitioner guides and how-tos AI network reference architectures: In Networking for AI inference model serving - GKE only and for all other backends , learn about reference architectures for AI inference model serving that provide centralized governance and private IP routing using Private Service Connect, Apigee API Management, and Model Armor. These architectures simplify multi-model scaling and prompt security across GKE, Cloud Run, and hybrid clouds. How-to guide: A Tale of TPU Observability on GKE: Part 2 - Dynamic Slicing Enhancements breaks down GKE's new Dynamic Slicing observability tools and metrics for next-generation v7 TPUs through an engaging, story-driven observability guide featuring Alex, a lead AI platform engineer. Explore the step-by-step diagnostic workflows with real-world examples and handy command-line snippets. Check out Part 1 here . Customer and partner updates AI21 achieves an 83% reduction in time-to-start for AI workloads with AI Hypercomputer : Frontier lab AI21 needed a new stack on which to train its Jamba family, and chose AI Hypercomputer configured with GKE on A3 and A3 Ultra instances. By doing so, AI21 says it cut high-priority job wait times from 72 hours to 12, and manual scheduling interventions from 20 per week to zero. Visko streams real-time world models on Google Cloud TPUs : Visko, an AI startup developing interactive world models, deployed an end-to-end live inference pipeline that combines video generation, super-resolution upscaling, and synchronized audio onto a single Cloud TPU slice . In this blog, the team discusses how it engineered the pipeline, the architectural optimizations it made, and practical lessons for other startups building ultra-low-latency generative AI. ZenteiQ scales physical AI inference 4x with GKE and llm-d : In order to pre-train models that understand physical laws, governing equations, and numerical solvers, Indian AI startup ZenteiQ designed and built a large-scale batch synthetic data-generation pipeline that runs across multiple model families and feeds verified datasets into training runs. GKE and GKE Inference Gateway gave ZenteiQ the inference-routing layer within its pipeline to scale aggregate inference throughput 4.07x and grow daily output from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion generated tokens for every 1,000 accelerators. Palo Alto Networks modernizes cloud-delivered security service : Palo Alto has worked with Google Cloud since 2018 to deliver its Prisma Access security service, and it was time to update it. In order not to compromise its security guarantees, Palo Alto separated the platform into two independently scalable layers: an ingress layer that handles traffic routing and forwarding running on GKE, with Axion C4A instances; and a security layer that handles threat inspection, running on dedicated single-tenant VMs fronted by an Internal Load Balancer. Each layer can now scale, update, and operate independently. title: When the Kubernetes API went silent: A three-layer networking mystery
raw_text:
Every support engineer has a case that stays with them. The one that comes up at team lunches. The one where, even after it's resolved, you find yourself staring at a packet capture at midnight just to make sure you really understand what happened. This is that case. It started in January 2026 with a support ticket that read deceptively simply: pods are intermittently failing to reach the Kubernetes API server. The error was a familiar-looking timeout. The customer had already ruled out their own operators. What none of us knew yet was that we were looking at three separate bugs — in three different layers of the stack — all conspiring to produce the same symptom at the same time. By the time it was over, around 800 developers had been blocked from deploying to production for weeks on end, and GKE clusters across europe-west had ground to a halt. In a race to fix the problem, we involved engineers across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, networking, hostnet, kernel, and the Linux upstream community, who together tracked down not one but three distinct root causes. And the final fix landed not as a config change or a feature flag, but as a patch to the Linux kernel itself. This is the story of how we got there. Part one: The alarm bell that wouldn't stop The customer ran a large multi-cluster GKE environment in Google Cloud's europe-west region. Their clusters used Private Service Connect — Google Cloud's mechanism for exposing the GKE control plane privately — and had a rich ecosystem of system-level workloads: Twistlock security scanners, External Secrets Operator for secrets management, Cilium for network policy, as well as several internal Kubernetes operators. The first errors appeared in one of its user acceptance testing (UAT) clusters in europe-west, and a few days later in a second cluster in the same region. They looked like this: Application logs — pods across multiple namespaces code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "TimeoutError: Connect call failed ('1.2.3.4', 443)
dial tcp 1.2.3.4:443: i/o timeout

# 1.2.3.4 is the cluster's internal VIP for the kube-apiserver,
# routed through Private Service Connect"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f55d90fbdd0>)])]> Initially the errors were intermittent — spikes in the logs, not a hard outage. The customer suspected their own code. Their team had recently deployed a custom operator built with the kopf framework, and it was the first thing they looked at. But the logs showed the errors had started eight days before the operator was ever deployed. When they shut it down completely, the timeouts kept coming. The issue persists even after completely scaling down the External Secrets Operator. The errors are appearing from customer workloads, and system-level pods we haven't touched. The growing list of suspects When a case like this arrives, the first instinct is to ask: what changed? The customer's timeline gave us several candidates, and we worked through them methodically. The custom operator (kopf): Ruled out immediately — errors predated deployment by a week and continued after shutdown. External Secrets Operator: Removed entirely on customer request. Timeouts continued in customer workloads that relied on Kubernetes control plane (KCP) connectivity, and cluster-internal system pods. Security agents: Uninstalled. Same result. We were now watching system-level Kubernetes components fail to reach their own control plane. conntrack table exhaustion: One theory was that too many half-open connections were filling the OS connection tracking table on the control plane nodes. We checked. The conntrack table was at roughly 50% capacity — of a default maximum of 1.3M entries. Not even close to exhaustion. Control plane overload: We scaled up the KCP VM size. kube-apiserver latencies looked healthy. No improvement on the timeout side. What made this case genuinely strange was the scope. We confirmed the timeouts were happening across five different clusters, affecting DaemonSets, Deployments, and system pods alike. External clients — developer laptops, GitHub Actions runners — were also hitting the same wall. This was not a broken workload. This was something wrong with the path between everything and the API server. The timeline so far Day 1: First I/O timeout errors appear (One of the UAT clusters in europe-west3. Intermittent, easy to dismiss.) Day 10: Errors become persistent (Frequency increases significantly. The issue is no longer dismissible.) Day 15: Case escalated — P0 bug filed (Multiple clusters confirmed affected. ~800 developers blocked. Production releases are frozen. Formal escalation begins.) Day 20: All obvious suspects ruled out (Custom operator, security agents, conntrack exhaustion, control plane resizing — all cleared.) Day 22: Packet captures collected (Captures taken simultaneously at the control-plane node NIC and from inside the kube-api container. The investigation enters its most critical phase.) With the obvious suspects cleared, and the scope undeniably wide, we did what you do when the application layer has nothing left to say: We went to the packets. Part two: Tracing the ghost in the wire To understand what the packet captures revealed, you first need to understand the architecture that a GKE pod traverses when it makes an API call. In a Private Service Connect-based GKE cluster, the path is deceptively long for something that looks like a local connection. (Note for formatting: Consider including the Pod → kube-apiserver flow diagram here: Pod -> Worker Node -> PSC NAT+Proxy -> ILB -> KCP VM NIC -> kube-apiserver) The key component here is Private Service Connect. When a pod dials 1.2.3.4:443 , it is not actually going directly to the control plane; that IP is a virtual endpoint. The connection is intercepted by Google's networking fabric, NAT'd through a Private Service Connect endpoint, passed through an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer, and ultimately delivered to the KCP VM, where Envoy acts as a local proxy in front of the actual kube-apiserver process. Private Service Connect adds a proxy protocol header to each new connection, so the kube-apiserver can see the real client IP. This will turn out to be important later. What the packets revealed When we captured simultaneously at the KCP VM's NIC (the PIGv interface, Google's programmable virtual NIC) and from inside the kube-apiserver container, we saw something striking. SYN packets from the pods were arriving at the KCP VM's NIC. They were getting that far. But instead of receiving a SYN-ACK in response — the expected second step of a TCP handshake — the client was getting back an out-of-place ACK. Not an RST. Not silence. An ACK that logically belonged to a different, earlier connection. Wireshark, the network protocol analyzer, was flagging these streams with a label that initially seemed innocuous: "TCP Port numbers reused." Wireshark — packet stream showing the failed handshake code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Time Source Port → Destination Port Info
09:13:41 10.0.13.77 53426 → 10.117.0.2 443 [SYN] Seq=0 Win=42600
09:13:41 10.117.0.2 443 → 10.0.13.77 53426 [SYN, ACK] Seq=0 Ack=1 Win=64768
 ... (data exchange, connection completes)
09:13:42 10.117.0.2 443 → 10.0.13.77 53426 [TCP Retransmission]
09:13:42 10.117.0.2 443 → 10.0.13.77 53426 [TCP Retransmission]
 ... (many retransmissions of the same ACK)

# 2 minutes later, same port 53426 is reused for a new connection
09:13:44 10.0.13.77 53426 → 10.117.0.2 443 [SYN] Seq=1498 ← NEW connection
 (expected: SYN-ACK)
 (received: ACK Seq=1498 Ack=1025 — belongs to PREVIOUS stream)
09:13:44 10.0.13.77 53426 → 10.117.0.2 443 [SYN] Retransmit...
09:13:44 10.0.13.77 53426 → 10.117.0.2 443 [SYN] Retransmit...
 → eventually: i/o timeout'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f55d90fa0d0>)])]> The pattern was clear. Something was causing the KCP VM to respond to a fresh SYN with an ACK that belonged to a different connection that had ended minutes ago . The old connection had used the same source port (53426 in the example above), and the KCP VM had never fully let go of it. "The KCP server sends FIN,ACK; client responds with FIN,ACK and then ACK. But KCP receives ACK before FIN,ACK. KCP server never ACKs the FIN,ACK — continuous retransmission of ACK. RST does not clear state." The "Invalid ACK" spike While one thread of the investigation was analyzing packet captures, a.k.a., pcaps, another team was digging into internal metrics for the Private Service Connect infrastructure — specifically the user space packet switch (USPS), Google's software switching layer that handles NAT and proxy protocol header injection for Private Service Connect connections. They found something alarming in the metrics for Andromeda, Google's networking fabric. A counter called "Proxy protocol drop: invalid ACK packet" had been flat for months — and then, in February 2026, it spiked sharply upward to several drops per second across the affected europe-west regions. That date matched a USPS version rollout. This version included a change which was a fix for a different bug but something about it had changed the behavior of how Private Service Connect handled a specific class of packet. Challenge ACKs: The RFC 5961 mechanism To understand the next piece of the puzzle, we need to talk about a TCP security mechanism called the challenge ACK, defined in RFC 5961. Imagine a TCP connection has closed — gone through the FIN/ACK dance and terminated. The server-side (here, the KCP VM) may still briefly remember the connection's sequence numbers in its TCP state machine. Now imagine that shortly afterward, a new client connection arrives on the same source port and destination port (the same 5-tuple). From the kernel's perspective, this could be a stale packet from the old connection, or it could be an attacker trying to inject data into what the kernel thinks is still an open session. RFC 5961 says: when you receive a SYN that matches an existing or recently-closed connection's remembered state, don't accept it blindly. Send a challenge ACK — an acknowledgment that carries the last known sequence number of the old connection. If the new client is legitimate, it will see this unexpected ACK, recognize the connection is stale, and send a RST to clear the state. The server then accepts the next SYN normally. The challenge ACK flow — how it's supposed to work code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Step 1: New client sends SYN on a reused port
Client → Server: SYN (seq=X, same 5-tuple as an old connection)

# Step 2: Server is in FIN_WAIT_2, sends challenge ACK
Server → Client: ACK (ack=old_seq — "is this really you?")

# Step 3: Client recognizes the stale state, resets it
Client → Server: RST

# Step 4: State is cleared. Server accepts the next SYN normally.
Client → Server: SYN (new connection)
Server → Client: SYN-ACK ← handshake succeeds'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f55d90f9990>)])]> This mechanism works perfectly — when the challenge ACK is allowed through . But that was exactly what the new USPS change was blocking. The culprit: A well-intentioned fix The change in USPS had been designed to fix a legitimate security issue in Private Service Connect's proxy protocol handling. Part of its effect was to drop packets it classified as "invalid ACKs" during the connection handshake phase — specifically, ACKs that arrived before the initial SYN-ACK had been sent, which in normal circumstances would be anomalous. Unfortunately, challenge ACKs look exactly like this: They arrive from the server before the new handshake has completed, in response to a SYN. From the USPS's new perspective, they looked like invalid packets. They were dropped silently. Why this broke GKE specifically: Private Service Connect uses NAT to share a single public endpoint across many client pods. This means many different pods — running on different nodes, from different namespaces — can all end up using the same source port after NAT, creating a high rate of 5-tuple collisions. The challenge ACK mechanism was being triggered far more often than it would be in a normal direct-connection scenario. The USPS fix hadn't introduced challenge ACKs — they had always been there. It had introduced the dropping of them, which broke a flow that GKE's TCP stack had silently depended on to clear stale state. Mitigation: Rolling back the change In February, we rolled back the USPS change , restoring the old behavior where challenge ACKs were passed through instead of dropped. The rate of "Proxy protocol drop: invalid ACK packet" dropped back toward baseline almost immediately. By early March , 2026, the customer confirmed that all affected clusters had recovered. No more timeout errors. But the rollback wasn't a fix. It was a band-aid. It restored the behavior the system had accidentally depended on . The deeper question — why was the KCP VM in FIN_WAIT_2 for over two minutes in the first place? — was still completely unanswered. That question led to Part 3. And it's where things got genuinely strange. Part three: Three bugs, one crime scene The mitigation bought us time, but it left a question hanging in the air: Why did the KCP VM keep connections in FIN_WAIT_2 for so long? A well-behaved TCP stack processes a FIN, acknowledges it, and closes the connection. The KCP VM was failing to do this, leaving half-open connections that persisted for more than two minutes — long enough for the port to be reused by Private Service Connect's NAT layer, long enough to cause the challenge ACK scenario we'd uncovered. To answer this, we needed to understand not just one bug, but three distinct failure modes that had intersected at the worst possible moment. Bug #1: Packet reordering at the PIGv The first piece was discovered through careful analysis of simultaneous captures at two points: the KCP VM's host NIC (inside the physical host running the VM) versus the PIGv — the virtual NIC as seen by the VM. At the host NIC level, packets arrived in perfect order. But by the time they crossed through USPS and appeared at the PIGv, they had been subtly reordered. This happens because of how Private Service Connect's miss-thread processing works. When Private Service Connect intercepts a new flow it hasn't seen before (a "miss"), it processes that packet through a slower path that adds the proxy protocol header and sets up NAT state. Subsequent packets in the same flow take a fast path. The consequence: a FIN or RST packet belonging to a flow in mid-close might arrive slightly out of order relative to the ACKs that followed it. What the KCP VM actually received (reordered sequence) code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "# What should have happened:
Client → Server: FIN, ACK (client initiates close)
Server → Client: ACK (server acknowledges client FIN)
Server → Client: FIN, ACK (server initiates its own close)
Client → Server: ACK (client acknowledges server FIN)
 → Connection fully closed. Both sides free.

# What the KCP VM actually received (reordered by PIGv/USPS):
Client → Server: ACK (arrives first — out of order)
Client → Server: FIN, ACK (arrives second, but kernel sees ACK first)
Server → Client: FIN, ACK (server sends close, enters FIN_WAIT_1)
Client → Server: FIN, ACK (old, now-reordered FIN from client)
 → Server should ACK this. But it doesn't..."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f55d90fa750>)])]> The reordering put the client's FIN after the server had already sent its own FIN. The server entered FIN_WAIT_1, then FIN_WAIT_2 after seeing the client's ACK of the server's FIN. But then the client's own FIN arrived — and the server's kernel ignored it. Bug #2: Envoy's half-close and the frozen timer Why couldn't the operating system clean up on its own? There is a Linux kernel parameter called tcp_fin_timeout that governs exactly this: how long a socket in FIN_WAIT_2 waits before being forcibly closed. On the KCP VM, this was set to 60 seconds. But tcp_fin_timeout only applies to orphaned sockets — sockets that no process is currently holding open. Envoy, the proxy that sits in front of kube-apiserver on the KCP VM, was performing a half-close: it called shutdown(SHUT_WR) , which closes the write side of the connection but keeps the socket open so it can still receive data. This is perfectly valid TCP behavior and is how graceful half-duplex termination is supposed to work. The side effect: As long as Envoy held the socket with SHUT_WR , the kernel did not consider it orphaned. tcp_fin_timeout never started. The socket sat in FIN_WAIT_2 indefinitely, waiting for a client FIN it would never be able to process correctly. # The kernel sees the new SYN on this 5-tuple and sends a challenge ACK.
# USPS drops the challenge ACK. → i/o timeout.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f55d90fa890>)])]> Bug #3: The Linux kernel's silent failure But there was still a missing piece. Even with the reordered FIN, a healthy kernel should still process a received FIN in FIN_WAIT_2 and move to TIME_WAIT . The socket should eventually close. Why wasn't it? This led us deep into the Linux TCP state-machine implementation. When the reordered client FIN arrived at the KCP VM, the kernel's tcp_ack() function was called to process it. And here, in kernel version 6.1 (which underpinned the Container-Optimized OS (COS) running on the KCP VMs), there was a bug. RFC 5961 added stricter validation for acceptable ACK numbers — specifically, an ACK could be considered valid even if it was slightly "old" (within a sequence number window), to handle network reordering. But in kernel 6.1, there was a code path where tcp_ack() returned zero — indicating "this packet was not fully processed" — when it encountered an ACK that was old but within the RFC 5961 acceptable window. The caller of tcp_ack() in the FIN processing path checked this return value, saw zero, and did… nothing. The FIN was received and silently discarded. The Linux kernel commit that fixed it (upstream) code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'commit 795a7dfbc3d9
Author: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
net: tcp: accept old ack during closing

tcp_ack() returns 0 when ack is old but acceptable wrt rfc5961.
In FIN_WAIT_2, this caused tcp_fin() to never be called for a
valid received FIN, leaving the connection stuck indefinitely.

Fixed: properly handle old-but-acceptable ACKs during connection close.
Introduced in 6.1, fixed in 6.9.7. LTS backports: 6.6.y and 6.1.y.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f55d90f89d0>)])]> The bug had existed since kernel 6.1 and was already fixed in kernel 6.9.7 — but GKE's KCP VMs were running COS builds based on 6.1 and 6.6. The fix needed to be backported and shipped as a COS image update. How the three bugs combined Individually, none of these three issues would have caused an outage of this magnitude. It took all three acting together to create the failure: Bug #1 alone: Packet reordering is mildly disruptive, but the kernel would normally still eventually process the FIN and clean up, just slower than ideal. Bug #2 alone: Envoy's half-close is perfectly correct behavior. It only becomes a problem if the FIN is never properly processed. Bug #3 alone: The kernel's failure to process old-but-acceptable ACKs would cause some connections to linger, but the impact would be limited without the port-reuse pressure from Private Service Connect NAT. All three together: Reordering causes the FIN to arrive out of sequence; the kernel bug prevents it from being processed; Envoy's SHUT_WR prevents the timeout from firing; the socket stays in FIN_WAIT_2 indefinitely. Private Service Connect NAT reuses the port. challenge ACK is sent. The USPS fix drops it. Connection fails. The resolution: A three-pronged fix Resolving this required action at three different levels, coordinated across multiple teams over several weeks: Immediate mitigation (Feb, 2026): Rollback of change in USPS. Restored the previous behavior where challenge ACKs were forwarded rather than dropped. Customer clusters recovered by early March. Correctness fix: A replacement change to handle the challenge ACK scenario properly in the Private Service Connect proxy protocol layer, rather than simply restoring the old drop behavior. A PacketDrill test was added to the test suite to prevent regression. Root cause fix — Linux kernel patch: Upstream patch ("net: tcp: accept old ack during closing"), authored by Eric Dumazet. Merged into Linux 6.9.7. Backported to 6.6.y and 6.1.y LTS branches. — shipping in GKE 1.33.5 and later. The bug is fully resolved at the OS level for all GKE versions running these COS images. What made this case different Most networking cases resolve at one layer. You find the misconfigured firewall rule, the exhausted connection pool, the miscalculated MTU. You fix it and move on. This one was different because the symptom — i/o timeout on a connection that never completed — was the same whether you were looking at the Private Service Connect layer, the kernel's TCP state machine, or Envoy's connection management. Every layer had a plausible explanation, and every explanation was incomplete. What finally cracked it was the discipline of simultaneous packet capture at multiple points in the path. Without captures at the host NIC, the PIGv, and inside the container at the same time, we would never have seen the reordering. Without correlating those pcaps to the USPS metric spike on February 18, we would never have found the dropped challenge ACKs. And without reproducing the issue in a lab environment, we would never have found the kernel bug that made the FIN_WAIT_2 state permanent. The other thing that made this work was the team. Over the course of two weeks, engineers from seven or eight different specialties contributed: GKE networking, Private Service Connect infrastructure, Hostnet, Andromeda, KCP, and ultimately the kernel community. No single person could have held all of this in their head. The case notes, the shared bug tracker, the meticulously collected pcaps — they were the connective tissue that let a distributed team work as one. In the end, the customer got back to production. The kernel got a better bug fix. And the rest of us got a very good story about why packet reordering, half-closed sockets, and a well-intentioned security patch should never be allowed in the same room at the same time. This blog is based on real case data from an anonymized customer support engagement and internal bugs. The Linux kernel fix referenced is commit 795a7dfbc3d9 , authored by Eric Dumazet. Special thanks to the engineers across GKE, Private Service Connect, Hostnet, Andromeda, COS, and the Linux networking community whose work made this resolution possible.

title: Innovate on your own business terms: Google Cloud spend caps now generally available
raw_text: Today, we’re announcing that spend caps on Google Cloud Budgets are generally available. With this release, we’re delivering ways to protect your workloads from runaway costs without risking resource deletion. More importantly, we’re introducing three major updates, directly inspired by your feedback since the initial preview, to bring programmability, real-time visibility, and automated guardrails to your cost-control playbook. How the new spend caps can help your business We have significantly enhanced the usability and power of spend caps in three ways: 1. Automation through spend caps API : Managing guardrails manually across hundreds of projects is a major operational challenge. To address this, we have launched the spend caps API, which can be accessed from the existing Cloud Billing Budgets API. You can now programmatically enforce your financial boundaries for eligible services within each project, without additional overhead. You can automatically lift, update, or delete caps on the fly and instantly apply a spend cap whenever a developer spins up a new sandbox project. 2. Real-time visibility with live cost reports: Spend caps for AI services trigger within minutes of usage using estimated, live costs. When a cap triggers, you need to know exactly why and when the limit was breached. You can now view these faster, estimated costs directly inside your Cost Reports. Instead of waiting hours for standard billing pipelines to settle net costs, you get the exact financial snapshots that triggered the enforcement, giving you the immediate context needed to run a precise root-cause analysis. 3. Automated guardrails for your monthly resets: Before, once a spend cap was triggered, the usage block remained locked until you manually lifted it in the UI. Today, we are introducing automated monthly resets. You no longer need to worry about manually lifting caps every month. Enforced spend caps will automatically reset, and blocked services will seamlessly resume at the beginning of the next month. However, if your governance policies require a strict manual audit before resuming operations, the manual override option continues to exist exactly as before. Best practices for deploying spend caps As you roll out spend caps across your organization, keep these operational tips in mind: Target non-production environments first : Start by applying strict, low-dollar spend caps to your developer sandboxes, testing clusters, and experimental AI agent playgrounds. Configure alerts wisely : Default alerts are automatically sent to billing administrators and project owners at 50%, 80%, and 100% of the cap. Make sure the right folks are set up in these roles. This ensures your team is never caught off guard when a budget is nearing depletion. Spend caps permissions can also be added to custom roles, if needed. Understand fixed vs on-demand costs : Spend caps halt pay-as-you-go and CUD-covered requests once the budget threshold is hit. However, Provisioned Throughput is never halted; requests using reserved capacity will continue to run, and serve traffic normally. Refresher on GCP’s dual-pronged defense playbook Spend Caps work seamlessly alongside our native Early Anomalies Detection to provide a closed-loop defense for your cloud spend. Read our previous blog for a detailed explanation on how to use these tools to effortlessly set up a GCP defense playbook. Playbook step Feature Focus Core action Key benefit Step 1 Early anomalies Predictive monitoring Analyzes early cost signals daily to alert you of directional spend variances Spot anomalous cost spikes early and pinpoint the exact SKU driving the trend Step 2 Spend caps Financial enforcement Programmatically pauses usage for a specific project/service once a budget is breached Absolute protection against runaway spend without deleting resources Get started today Spend caps are now ready to support your workloads at scale. Read our documentation for more details and navigate to the Budgets and Alerts page in your Google Cloud Billing Console, to set your first spend cap. To integrate programmatic guardrails into your deployment workflows, check out our newly published spend caps API documentation .

title: Choosing a WAAP in 2026: 3 questions that separate the shortlist
raw_text: One platform or four Your WAF renewal is coming up. The API team has its own tooling in mind, the fraud team wants a bot product, and someone in networking owns DDoS. Four controls, four consoles, four sets of policies in front of the same applications. That is the situation a Web Application and API Protection platform, or WAAP, exists to replace: one service in front of the application portfolio that handles the WAF, API security, bot management, DDoS, and client-side script protection together. The category is settled. What changed in 2026 is the evidence. Buyers now have certified test data that measures how well these platforms stop attacks and how often they stop legitimate traffic by mistake, and the two numbers together tell you more than any feature list. What the test data shows The SecureIQLab Cloud WAAP v5.0 validation, an AMTSO-certified test published in August 2026, ran 12 enterprise platforms through 1,608 attack scenarios and 1,487 legitimate-traffic scenarios. Complete Security Scores ran from a perfect 100% for the top product down to roughly 61% for the weakest. The spread inside a typical shortlist is that wide, and a shortlist drawn up in 2023 or 2024 may no longer describe the products on it. The second number matters as much as the first. A platform that blocks every attack and also blocks legitimate requests cannot stay in blocking mode for long, and false positive avoidance varied almost as widely across the same twelve products. Those percentage points become alerts, tuning hours, and exceptions your team carries every day. 3 questions for every vendor on the list Ask for API coverage protocol by protocol. REST is one protocol among several in a modern estate; GraphQL, SOAP, WebSockets, and gRPC all carry production traffic, and the v5.0 results showed coverage varying widely by protocol inside a single product, with WebSockets the weakest area across the group. A headline API score hides that. Ask how long it takes to reach a tuned, low false-positive state on your traffic, and measure it over two full weeks of real traffic during the proof of value. Time to protection and tuning effort are the costs you pay after the contract is signed. Ask how the deployment and licensing model behaves as the portfolio grows. Each delivery model, SaaS, native in-cloud, or reverse proxy, has its own latency and onboarding profile, and each licensing unit, request, bandwidth, or application, bends the cost curve differently as traffic grows. Model 24 to 36 months of growth with each vendor, starting from your own traffic baseline. In the SecureIQLab v5.0 cycle, Imperva was the only vendor of the twelve tested to record a perfect 100% Complete Security Score, and it paired that with a 100% false positive avoidance score, the lab’s measure of legitimate traffic passed untouched. It was Imperva’s fifth consecutive Leader-category placement in the series, and the lab awarded it the Secure by Default rating in the same cycle. Forrester named Imperva a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: Web Application Firewall Solutions, Q1 2025. An honest aside: no one platform suits every environment. If your dominant requirement is a developer-centric edge platform or raw DDoS scrubbing capacity above everything else, weigh those needs explicitly, and validate any shortlist, Imperva included, against your own traffic in a proof of value. title: Why identity governance demands executive attention
raw_text: The identity landscape you’re responsible for looks nothing like it did just a few years ago. Employees and contractors now share the enterprise with service accounts, machine identities, and a fast-growing population of AI agents — all accessing business systems and data. Every one of those identities represents an access decision, and every access decision is now a potential point of accountability that lands on your desk. Regulators and boards want proof. They expect security leaders to show who, or what, has access to critical systems and how that access is being governed. But when human and nonhuman identities (NHIs) change faster than manual processes can keep up, proof becomes much harder to produce. Foundry research ranks identity security among the top cybersecurity priorities for 2026, reflecting a shift in how leadership views risk: Identity has evolved from operational detail to executive concern. “The last 15 years of digital transformation has resulted in credential sprawl across the tech stack of every organization,” says Bryan Kelley, AVP, Agentic Technology Specialists at SailPoint. “Whether it’s your own trusted agents or another organization’s rogue agent, they will find and abuse these exposed credentials, API keys, tokens, and secrets to carry out their given goals.” When accountability becomes personal Security leaders must demonstrate that identity governance is working, not simply that policies exist. They need a real-time view of each identity and the permissions it holds as business needs change. Leaders can also face personal and professional consequences when a breach or a compliance failure occurs. Boards and regulators may expect the C-suite to show that appropriate controls and oversight were in place at the time. AI agents add to that exposure as they gain access to enterprise resources and take on more autonomous roles. This is why NHIs need the same rigor, visibility, and controls as human identities. The shift to continuous compliance Quarterly or annual access reviews capture a moment in time, but it’s all the other moments in between that present a problem. Between reviews, employees can change roles, contractors can leave, and new identities such as AI agents can gain access. Security teams may not catch outdated permissions or active orphaned accounts until the next review. When identity data lives in separate systems, security teams struggle even more to maintain a current view of access across the enterprise . Continuous identity security makes oversight part of daily operations. Rather than waiting for the next review, an identity governance platform can help validate access as conditions change, automating low-risk approvals and flagging higher-risk access for review. Governance activity also creates an ongoing record of how access was approved and whether policies were applied consistently, so teams don’t have to reconstruct that history when auditors or regulators ask for evidence. Building an adaptive identity security program A continuous approach is made up of three core capabilities. First, organizations need to discover and unify identities to create a centralized view of access. Second, lifecycle management, policy enforcement, and access validation become always-on activities rather than periodic projects. Finally, organizations need to maintain evidence of governance activity so they can demonstrate compliance and respond when issues arise. This approach helps security leaders keep up with constant identity changes while meeting rising expectations for accountability. title: Anthropic AI model finds Linux kernel bug that leads to remote root access
raw_text: Linux servers running Multipath TCP (MPTCP) could be vulnerable to remote code execution through a flaw in the kernel’s networking stack. Anthropic has disclosed a zero-click exploit developed with an unreleased Claude research model that allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root, without requiring any user interaction. Tracked as CVE-2026-98432 , the vulnerability is a race-condition-induced use-after-free (UAF) bug in the Linux kernel. Anthropic demonstrated how an attacker could exploit the flaw remotely to leak kernel memory, defeat Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), hijack kernel control flow, and ultimately execute an attacker-controlled shell command. The research is part of Anthropic’s broader effort to evaluate AI models’ ability to discover and exploit vulnerabilities in widely deployed software. The company disclosed five exploit chains involving Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux to demonstrate how its internal model could combine multiple weaknesses into functional attacks. Anthropic’s proof of concept for the Linux exploit took approximately 53 minutes to progress from the initial memory leak to successful root-level command execution, the company said in a blog post . A TCP connection race leaves kernel memory exposed According to a Linux kernel CVE advisory , the underlying flaw involves how Linux manages IP options during IPv4 TCP connection establishment. When a new connection is created, the kernel can transfer ownership of IP options from a pending connection request to the newly created socket without making a separate copy. The problem arises when another CPU is simultaneously processing a retransmitted connection request and using those same options to construct a synchronize-acknowledge (SYNACK) response. If the child socket is freed before the second CPU finishes accessing the options, the kernel can end up reading memory that has already been released. This creates a use-after-free condition. The upstream fix addresses the memory-management problem by deferring the release of the affected objects until after a read-copy-update (RCU) grace period, giving concurrent readers time to finish accessing them. The flaw received a critical severity score of 9.8 and affects eight Linux kernel branches, dating back to version 4.4. Fixed releases include 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3-rc7. For users who obtain Linux through distributions such as Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE, and Amazon Linux, fixed kernel packages are available for at least some releases. Ubuntu and Red Hat Enterprise Linux, however, had yet to release patched kernels as of October 30. MCTCP listeners create the remote attack surface Anthropic’s exploit specifically targets Linux servers running an MPTCP listener. MPTCP extends conventional TCP by allowing a device to use multiple network interfaces simultaneously within a single connection. This enables bandwidth aggregation, improved network selection, and failover when one network path becomes unavailable. Linux implements MPTCP through its networking stack, but the protocol is opt-in: applications must explicitly request it when creating sockets, although mechanisms such as eBPF and other configuration techniques can also force applications to use it. Administrators are advised to review their kernel versions, apply the relevant security updates, and assess whether their systems expose MPTCP listeners.

title: Will artificial intelligence spell the end for SaaS?
raw_text:
The deployment of software-as-a-service (SaaS) has defined the past decade, as organisations moved away from managing network infrastructure towards a service-led model. Using SaaS requires less configuration and installation, as well as less demand for specialist talent and skills. This means teams can focus their energy on building applications and features that drive revenue.

Now, as organisations deploy artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities across the enterprise, attention is turning towards what is already being used. Will the next generation of SaaS market leaders be those that own the customer journey from end to end, using AI to connect workflows rather than simply add another intelligent feature? Or will SaaS be defined less by software capabilities and more by how effectively platforms integrate with and orchestrate business processes?

If this is the disruption being caused by AI, then as capabilities become easier to replicate, competitive advantage is shifting away from feature lists and towards owning entire customer workflows. Essentially, is AI disrupting what makes SaaS valuable, or is it commoditising the features that once differentiated these platforms?

George Brocklehurst, a research vice-president in the emerging tech and trends research practice at Gartner, says that over the past 12-18 months, we’ve seen a progressive shift from a question-and-answer model towards AI-enabled workflows designed to achieve a business outcome, where the model becomes a component in a more composite system.

He explains that, in its current direction, AI will not simply update traditional SaaS, but is “truly rendering the dashboard UI [user interface] experiences obsolete”. Therefore, the next generation of SaaS is not going to be defined by software capabilities, but by orchestrating cross-domain workflows for end-to-end outcomes.

Is AI disrupting what made SaaS valuable by commoditising the features that once offered differentiation? Brocklehurst says AI is being used to connect workflows more effectively, rather than simply adding more features.

“This is how leading-edge agentic solutions are gaining scale in enterprises,” he says. “Lots of enterprises are dabbling in it, trialling it, failing with it, but where it’s gaining traction is where those solutions better interpret context and retain institutional knowledge. The key takeaway here is that the threat to SaaS incumbents isn’t this full sci-fi autonomy, it’s unifying capability.”

  • Interview: Oracle NetSuite’s Evan Goldberg – SaaS-pocalypse averted: The executive vice-president of Oracle NetSuite discusses the evolution of AI in SaaS ERP, countering any SaaS-pocalypse narrative, citing an ecosystem knowledge edge.
  • SaaS-pocalypse? Maybe not, but SaaS applications are changing: It’s unlikely that SaaS is undergoing an extinction-level event, IT leaders say, but AI is disrupting software in ways that enterprises must learn to navigate effectively.

Brocklehurst says leading agentic services are progressively arbitraging this market (exploiting the difference between what tasks currently cost and what AI agents can deliver), while suppliers focusing their R&D on making individual users faster inside their own stacks are going to be fighting for commodity pennies.

“These are stateless tools that miss or forget that business context the minute the session ends,” he says.

“The user doesn’t want to log in to five different dashboards to pull a report: they want a single unified agentic layer that does the heavy lifting for them across those systems.”

Brocklehurst explains that a user can collect data points from different SaaS stacks and use AI to bring them together into deliverables. “The moment that an agent sits between the user and the software, the legacy application becomes headless,” he says.

Fatigue by training?

Brocklehurst says surveys conducted by Gartner show that enterprise buyers are fatigued by AI, and buyers don’t want to be sold another tool that their team needs to learn. They just need the tool to “deliver business value, automate the outcomes and make it work across the stacks”.

He says that once an agentic service can customise how it interacts with users based on personal, functional and organisational relevance, those interactions become more relevant.

“They reduce friction in working with the technology, and that earns you the right to operate across multiple domains,” says Brocklehurst. “It builds trust. In other surveys that we’ve done, trust drives the frequency of engagement, and so as you more frequently engage with the technology and get to better outcomes, that drives the return on investment.”

He says this is helping to scale enterprise adoption, as every time you introduce something that makes a workflow more fragmented, it adds more friction. What we see is that those providers and platforms that absorb that adaptation tax unlock fragmented value streams that stretch across the enterprise.

No value in SaaS?

The rise of AI is beginning to challenge the traditional SaaS model, with Forrester describing a potential “SaaS-pocalypse” for suppliers that cannot demonstrate clear value in an AI-first world.

It says that horizontal point-solution providers are particularly exposed, especially where products have low switching costs, limited integration into enterprise workflows and an unclear return on investment.

While some AI-native suppliers may also be acquired by larger technology companies as the market consolidates, larger enterprise SaaS providers are responding by embedding AI agents into their existing platforms and moving towards AI-first business models.

Their advantage lies in established enterprise relationships, industry expertise, data, consulting ecosystems, and the ability to combine technology with processes and governance. However, even these suppliers could face disintermediation as AI orchestration, control and semantic data layers increasingly sit above traditional application suites.

Merrick Lackner, CEO of Rently, says we are not on the way to a SaaS-pocalypse. Rather than SaaS being dead, he says, we will see a more in-depth network of partnerships emerge.

“We’ve seen Anthropic and Salesforce announce this partnership where they’re able to mutually benefit each other, and I think we’re going to continue to see that,” says Lackner.

“When it comes to just purely agentic services synthesising information, that does become increasingly commoditised,” he adds. “You can get that kind of service through OpenAI, through Gemini, through Anthropic, and of course, as a business, you could wrap that into your service as well with one of those providers or with your own foundation model.”

Fitting into AI

For organisations buying SaaS, this means reassessing how their existing applications fit into a wider AI strategy, rather than simply adding more point solutions. Companies will need to rationalise their SaaS estates, address technical debt, establish better data governance, and understand which capabilities genuinely differentiate the business and which could increasingly be replicated by AI.

Contracts may also need to change, moving away from traditional seat-based pricing towards consumption- or outcome-based models as AI agents become part of enterprise software.

How does this affect existing security suppliers and service providers? Lackner says that if you look at firms such as Zscaler and CrowdStrike, or companies such as Salesforce, they have tremendous amounts of data, and we know that even the frontier models have reached the point where they can ingest publicly available information.

“I think we’re going into a world of partnership, so I think they’re going to mutually enhance one another,” he says. “AI tools are great at synthesising information, but then there’s specialised information, too. So, when it comes to specialised information, the route to go is definitely with mutually beneficial arrangements.”

Lackner also says the addition of AI services will allow providers to use transformer technology to sift through and analyse data, and come up with solutions based on it.

“Prior to a partnership, a frontier or foundation model may not have access to all that data,” he says. “Then these partnerships get constructed where the data can be viewed in whatever silos or repositories, and then act on it.

“Being plugged into data sources and so forth is basically making certain repositories of information available that AI and GenAI [generative AI] would not necessarily have readily available.”

Autonomous modification

Forrester says that as legacy systems, commercial software and large open-source estates were not designed for autonomous modification, organisations must remain cautious about allowing AI to make large-scale changes without oversight.

Rather than simply replacing existing security testing tools, the shift could instead favour integrated software development platforms where security, validation and remediation are built into the development process. This puts greater emphasis on tools and controls that can provide context, constrain AI-driven changes and validate that remediation is safe.

Lackner says that as more companies build their own foundation models, while also partnering for sophisticated tasks that require greater depth and complexity with frontier models, learning and security will be at the forefront.

“My personal opinion is that’s going to be done through partnerships in the coming decade, for sure, but I’m still of the opinion that humans are driving a big portion of this,” he says.

“AI is not sentient and conscious, you know, in the same way that a human is, and even as a matter of first principle, whatever an AI does, it does need to get an instruction. Even in recursive development, there is an initial instruction set that comes from people.”

AI may not spell the end of SaaS, but it is likely to change what users expect from it, shifting value away from individual features, and towards the ability to connect data, applications and workflows. The SaaS platforms that thrive may therefore be those that become less visible to users, providing the underlying intelligence, data and infrastructure that AI agents need to deliver business outcomes.

title: AI and education: Learning to dance – Computer Weekly Downtime Upload podcast
raw_text:
In this episode, Paul Roehrig, chief strategy and marketing officer at software engineering services firm Ascendion, discusses artificial intelligence (AI) in education with Brian McKenna, enterprise applications editor at Computer Weekly.

Their conversation explores how students and teachers can prepare for a future increasingly shaped by generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), and how we can benefit from AI without surrendering intellectual autonomy.

The discussion begins with a fundamental question: what should students learn today to prepare for a world that cannot yet be fully described? Paul explains how this question arose repeatedly during the book tour for his co-authored 2017 book What to do when machines do everything.

A common assumption back then, nearly a decade ago, was that learning computer programming would be the best preparation for an AI-driven future. However, he argues that the more important skills for many people are not necessarily technical but intellectual and human.

As AI becomes increasingly pervasive, people must learn to work effectively with machines as intellectual partners. Paul describes this relationship as learning to “dance” with technology. Rather than simply accepting machine-generated answers, people need to develop critical thinking and intellectual curiosity, he says.

Education must therefore teach students how to recognise what constitutes a good answer and assess evidence.

Large language models (LLMs) can access and process enormous quantities of information, far beyond what an individual could read or memorise, notes Paul. But they have significant limitations. They lack human context and do not interpret information in the same way people do. Their responses are generated from patterns learned from existing material, which may be ineluctably flawed.

Paul emphasises that AI systems reflect human knowledge and behaviour. We made them, after all. Their biases and errors are therefore not separate from humans. They can reproduce shortcomings that are embedded in the very information on which they are trained. Therefore, users must learn to recognise these limitations rather than treating machine-generated responses as unquestionable facts.

This makes critical evaluation an essential educational skill. Students should be able to identify hallucinations and challenge unsupported claims.

Brian observes that the introduction of GenAI in schools has produced mixed results. Reporting by Computer Weekly has highlighted both positive opportunities, including the potential to level the playing field for learners, and concerns about its implementation. Brian adds that teachers and teaching unions are particularly concerned about the possible de-skilling of educators and the implications of relying excessively on automated systems.

Paul remains optimistic. He sees AI as a tool that can improve writing and help people think more effectively. However, the benefits depend on how the technology is used.

The principal danger lies in the outsourcing of human autonomy, he says. If learners surrender their curiosity to machines, they risk becoming passive consumers of automated answers. In response to Brian, Paul warns against an educational future in which humans merely maintain machines rather than exercise independent thought.

He argues that AI should complement effective teaching, not replace it. Simply introducing tools such as ChatGPT into classrooms and expecting children to learn how to use them independently is unlikely to succeed.

Brian and Paul muse on whether generative AI represents a fundamental departure from earlier educational technologies, such as calculators, word processors and traditional search engines. Paul acknowledges that AI is qualitatively different because it can enhance cognition and help users explore ideas in ways earlier tools could not.

But he does see important similarities with previous technological developments. Technologies have, time and again, generated debates about whether they improve learning or undermine established abilities.

Paul compares an LLM to a library containing an immense body of knowledge. Whereas humans cannot read and absorb everything in a library, AI can retrieve and process all that information rapidly.

He believes history offers grounds for optimism. People have repeatedly learned to use new technologies productively, despite initial fears. A positive outcome is possible, he maintains, but it is not guaranteed.

The Swedish case

The conversation highlights the renewed interest in traditional educational methods, including reading physical books, writing by hand and solving mathematical problems with pencil and paper. Brian mentions Sweden, a digitally advanced society where there has been interest in returning to more analogue approaches in education, as reported on by the BBC.

Paul supports the underlying principle, but he rejects the idea that these methods are merely old-fashioned. Human cognition has remained broadly consistent over thousands of years, and educational practices that develop knowledge and critical reasoning remain relevant, he says.

Reading longer works and engaging deeply with literature can provide the intellectual foundations needed to evaluate information. Paul rejects the suggestion that short-form social media content, such as on TikTok, can provide everything people need to understand the world. Students require a shared grounding in literature, inquiry and critical thinking to become discerning consumers of information.

He also stresses that traditional education itself can evolve. Teaching materials should, for instance, include societally under-represented perspectives and address embedded biases. Preserving valuable educational practices does not mean resisting improvement, he maintains – it means retaining the foundations that help people think independently.

Brian asks whether an 18-year-old would still be well advised to study computer science at university as in recent decades, and Paul answers “Yes”. The world will continue to need skilled programmers, computer scientists and people capable of building and maintaining AI systems, he maintains.

However, he argues that the bar for success has risen. Mediocre programmers working on relatively straightforward tasks may find their work increasingly supplemented or replaced by AI. The strongest career prospects belong to people who can solve complex problems and reason systematically but also be emotionally intelligent.

At the same time, both Brian and Paul say they believe the humanities are more important than ever. Literature, philosophy and other humanities disciplines can help people understand different perspectives and reflect on what it means to be human.

The two discuss whether AI has effectively given everyone an additional 20 IQ points since generative AI became prominent in November 2022. Paul rejects the suggestion that human brains have been rewired or that people have necessarily become smarter.

Next time around, Paul and Brian will discuss Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel Klara and the Sun, exploring how it treats the interaction between humans and machines.

title: UK extends facial recognition to civil immigration offences
raw_text:
UK Immigration Enforcement will be able to deploy live facial recognition (LFR) technology outside of border zones to look for people who have never committed a criminal offence, prompting concern from digital rights groups about surveillance overreach.

The concerns were triggered after the Home Office published policy and impact assessment documents that say Immigration Enforcement’s use of LFR surveillance will extend beyond ports of entry to the UK, as well as stray into civil rather than criminal matters.

A new policy document published on 8 October 2026, for example, set out rules for how Immigration Enforcement should approach its LFR deployments – including watchlist creation, approved locations, human oversight measures and biometric matching thresholds – but also covers how to conduct facial recognition operations beyond ports of entry to the UK.

Under the guidance, this means Immigration Enforcement may deploy LFR at transport hubs, events that are “expected to increase footfall at a location” and along travel routes.

It also covers joint deployments with police forces, allowing Immigration Enforcement to supply watchlists for police facial recognition systems, or otherwise process police-supplied data through its own systems.

Accompanying the policy document is a data protection impact assessment (DPIA), published on 22 October 2026, which notes that LFR could be used to support “administrative or civil immigration activity” rather than being used solely for criminal matters, which operate under a different set of more stringent legal rules.

This means people could be included on LFR watchlists for overstaying a visa, working without permission, or entering without leave, all of which are considered civil rather than criminal matters.

The publication of LFR documents by the Home Office follows eight “trial” LFR deployments by Immigration Enforcement at Holyhead port in November 2025, which scanned 5,474 faces but led to only a single arrest. A second set of 10 “trial” deployments from February 2026 at the same location scanned 2,752 faces and resulted in two arrests.

Taken together, the documents suggest that Immigration Enforcement could routinely deploy LFR outside of border zones – particularly when attached to wider police LFR deployments that regularly take place on high streets or at events – to look for people who have not committed any criminal offences.

Computer Weekly has also heard concerns about data quality and integrity issues in the underlying database from which Immigration Enforcement will draw facial images for its LFR watchlists, as this is the same database that underpins the Home Office’s error-prone electronic visa (eVisa) system.

These issues include profile mismatches – where people are, for example, shown incorrect personal details or given wrong visa expiry dates – and immigration statuses becoming “entangled” with other people’s records.

In terms of LFR, this means an individual could be included in an Immigration Enforcement watchlist if the underlying system entangles their identity records with someone else’s.

Computer Weekly contacted the Home Office about every aspect of the story – including concerns shared by civil society about the expansion of LFR surveillance into non-criminal matters, and how the department is dealing with data integrity issues when creating watchlists – but received no response by the time of publication.

Civil society reactions

Responding to the publication of the documents, Jake Hurfurt, head of research and investigations at privacy group Big Brother Watch, noted the “broad” language used gives the UK government “worrying latitude to use this Orwellian technology” to target an ever-growing number of people.

“It is shocking to see the Home Office quietly set itself up for yet another massive expansion of facial recognition use in this country. It is a difference in kind to use it to identify people they suspect of administrative, rather than criminal, breaches of the law,” he said.

“Police use of this technology has seen repeated false alerts. What will happen when an algorithm malfunction or dodgy Home Office data leads to someone being wrongly accused of breaching immigration rules? The UK is not a ‘papers please’ society where we all carry ID, but this threatens to turn our streets not just into a police lineup, but a border control booth as well.”

According to a recent research report by the Open Rights Group (ORG) – which looked at the use of technologies with artificial intelligence (AI) throughout the UK’s border control ecosystem, including LFR – while it is promising that the government is actively publishing guidelines and policy documents, “no safeguard is good enough to avoid the normalisation of mass surveillance in democratic settings”.

It added that the only effective safeguard against abuse of AI and biometric surveillance is to reject the security framing around migration that paints people on the move as a threat, and to “ensure that AI and automation serve humanitarian, not carceral purposes”.

The ORG concluded that the increasing normalisation of surveillance is not just a problem for migrants: “The hostile environment, once automated, becomes a template for governance across society. The very technologies and rationales deployed at the border quickly find their way into domestic policing and public spaces, transforming everyone into a potential suspect.”

Watchlist creation concerns

While the Immigration Enforcement LFR DPIA notes that a separate impact assessment has been carried out to cover watchlist creation in more detail, the document has yet to appear online with the other published materials. The Home Office did not respond to questions on when it would be published.

Wider police LFR deployments carry a number of issues with watchlist creation, including that the main source of facial images for these systems – the Police National Database (PND) – still contains millions of unlawfully held custody images. While the High Court ordered the Home Office to destroy the unlawfully retained images in 2012, the department has yet to do so.

However, the existing DPIA does note that “for joint deployments, any sharing of watchlist data with police forces or other partners will be governed by a deployment-specific data sharing arrangement”, which will set out the purpose of the sharing, its legal basis, data controller or processor roles, watchlist criteria, security arrangements, data retention and deletion requirements, and audit responsibilities.

Aside from potential data from the PND, the documents published so far confirm that Immigration Enforcement will use a number of other databases as sources of facial images.

“All data held is derived from Home Office systems, such as the Person Centric Data Platform (PCDP), Atlas [a case working system], Immigration and Biometrics System (IABS), Central Reference System (CRS) and Initial Status Assessment (ISA), and reflects data held in those live systems, being updated via a regular data feed,” said the DPIA.

The PCDP in particular brings a number of concerns. This database acts as a centralised service that bridges different datasets to consolidate identity records and migration statuses for the UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI) View and Prove online service, which underpins the Home Office’s eVisa system.

Given the data quality and integrity issues present with the eVisa system, there is concern about how this translates to its use in LFR if people’s identity records become entangled by the system and are then included in the watchlists.

Speaking with Computer Weekly, migrant support group the3million said it is worried about the Home Office expanding digital border enforcement when its own systems have been shown to hold incorrect data that it struggles to find and fix.

“In June, the Home Office confirmed that a group of EU Settlement Scheme status holders had eVisas that did not show their correct status,” said Kaelynn Narita, research and policy manager at the3million. “If the Home Office builds watchlists from these same databases, errors could lead to people being wrongly flagged, stopped or questioned, or struggling to prove their rights when they return to the UK.

“Before using this data to target people, the Home Office must be open about how it identifies and corrects errors in its caseworking systems.”

Another aspect of police LFR that has come under criticism is the gap between rhetoric and practice, as while the Home Office and individual police forces claim the technology is reserved for only serious criminality, watchlists have previously included people for shoplifting, drug, or traffic offences that do not meet the legal threshold of serious crime.

Writing in a September 2025 research paper about the “wild west” of police facial recognition testing, academics Karen Yeung and Wenlong Li noted that while the Metropolitan Police’s watchlists were populated by individuals wanted on outstanding arrest warrants, they also included “images of a much broader, amorphous category of persons” who did not meet the definition of serious offenders.

Computer Weekly contacted the Home Office about what processes are in place to identify and correct errors in its caseworking systems and databases, but again received no response.

A new legal framework?

As it stands, police use of facial recognition is regulated through a “patchwork” legal framework, although the King’s Speech in May 2026 confirmed new legal rules would be contained within the upcoming Police Reform Bill.

When launching its consultation on a new framework for the tech in December 2025, the Home Office said the current rules governing police LFR use are “complicated and difficult to understand”, and that an ordinary member of the public would be required to read four pieces of legislation, police national guidance documents and a range of detailed legal or data protection documents from individual forces to fully understand the basis for LFR use on their high streets.

Computer Weekly contacted the biometric and surveillance camera commissioner for England and Wales, William Webster, about the expansion of LFR into the immigration enforcement sphere.

He confirmed that while he was aware of the pilots, his remit primarily covers police forces and local authorities, and does not extend to immigration services.

“I have argued, in my response to the Home Office consultation on LFR and other biometric surveillance use, that the new proposed legislative framework should apply to all public services, including the NHS, public transport, immigration and prisons, etc. I have also argued that the government should give serious consideration to extending the legislative framework to the commercial sector, such as retailers,” he said.

“We won’t know the scope of coverage until the Police Reform Bill is laid before Parliament, but I am hopeful that in the future a new regulatory body, which will replace my office and which will have stronger compliance powers, will regulate the use of biometric surveillance technologies by immigration services.”

Webster added that the trials of LFR by Immigration Enforcement highlight “the urgent need for a legislative framework which sets out tests and rules for necessity and proportionality in primary legislation”.

In a recent interview with former prime minister Tony Blair, home secretary Shabana Mahmood described her ambition to use technologies such as AI and LFR to achieve Jeremy Bentham’s vision of a “panopticon”, referring to his proposed prison design that would allow a single, unseen guard to silently observe every prisoner at once.

Typically used today as a metaphor for authoritarian control, the underpinning idea of the panopticon is that by instilling a perpetual sense of being watched among the inmates, they would behave as authorities wanted.

“When I was in justice, my ultimate vision for that part of the criminal justice system was to achieve, by means of AI and technology, what Jeremy Bentham tried to do with his panopticon,” Mahmood told Blair. “That is that the eyes of the state can be on you at all times.”
